notes.meaning: Israel begins this chapter by looking back at the lands they won east of the Jordan River before entering Canaan. This territory stretched all the way from the deep Arnon gorge in the south to snowy Mount Hermon in the north. Remembering past victories helps believers trust that the God who helped them before will help them again.

Sihon king of the Amorites had ruled from the Arnon gorge up to the Jabbok River, which covered half of the fertile region of Gilead. His realm also took in the Jordan valley plains stretching from the Sea of Galilee down to the Dead Sea. Even though Sihon was entrenched in his capital at Heshbon, God gave his entire realm to Israel.

Og king of Bashan was a ruler of giant stature who governed the northern lands up to Mount Hermon from his royal cities of Ashtaroth and Edrei. His territory included the rest of Gilead and bordered neighboring nations to the far north. Despite his terrifying reputation and strong cities, he fell before God's people just like Sihon did.

Moses led Israel to conquer these two powerful kingdoms and gave the captured land to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. Recalling Moses honors the faithful servant God used before Joshua took over leadership. God often works through different leaders in different seasons to accomplish His unchanging plan.

Joshua led the nation to conquer the territory west of the Jordan River, from Mount Lebanon in the far north to Mount Halak near Edom in the south. This region included all types of landscapes—mountains, foothills, fertile valleys, and dry wilderness—belonging to six distinct nations. God gave all of it to the remaining tribes of Israel as an inheritance, exactly as He had promised.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars compare this detailed list to ancient Near Eastern victory monuments, which kings set up to officially record conquered lands and show the success of their campaigns.

notes.meaning: The list of kings defeated by Joshua begins with Jericho and Ai, the first two cities taken after Israel crossed the Jordan River. It continues with Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, and Lachish, the leading southern cities that joined together to fight against Israel. No human alliance can stand when God decides it is time to bring down proud kingdoms.

This group includes the southern kings of Eglon, Gezer, Debir, Geder, Hormah, and Arad. Several of these leaders had marched out to rescue other cities under attack, but each was met with defeat. Their downfalls proved that trusting in neighboring allies cannot save anyone from God's judgment.

Israel defeated the kings of Libnah, Adullam, Makkedah, Bethel, Tappuah, and Hepher throughout the central and western foothills. Cities like Adullam and Bethel had ancient histories, but their fortresses could not withstand the Lord's army. God methodically broke every stronghold that held the land captive to idolatry.

Moving into northern Canaan, Israel defeated the kings of Aphek, Lasharon, Madon, Hazor, Shimron-meron, and Achshaph. Hazor was the chief city of the north and had gathered a massive coalition with iron chariots, yet God gave them into Joshua's hands in a single battle. God's strength always overcomes even the most overwhelming odds.

The record moves through northern fortresses and coastlands, naming the kings of Taanach, Megiddo, Kedesh, Jokneam, Dor, and Goiim in Gilgal. These cities controlled major travel routes and fertile valleys across the land. By subduing each ruler, God opened every corner of the country so His people could receive their homes.

The last king listed is the ruler of Tirzah, bringing the grand total of defeated western kings to thirty-one. In those days, a king ruled just one city and its surrounding farmland rather than an entire empire. Writing down every single king showed the Israelites that God had completely fulfilled His covenant promise to give them the land.

differ.view: Some evangelicals explain that while Joshua broke the military power of all thirty-one kings, individual tribes still faced the task of clearing out the remaining Canaanites from their local settlements.
